Mohawk

Kanien’kehá:ka, commonly called Mohawk, includes multiple communities and governing institutions. This guide uses Akwesasne’s council and museum publications alongside a Six Nations language study as clearly scoped examples, rather than treating one government as representative of all Mohawk people.

Read the sources [3] Mohawk Council of Akwesasne [5] Six Nations Polytechnic

01

Identity and context

Mohawk, also described through Kanien’kehá:ka, is one of the Haudenosaunee nations with multiple distinct communities.

Read the sources [1] quebec.ca

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Community governments, language and cross-border homelands. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] quebec.ca [2] quebec.ca

03

Akwesasne and imposed boundaries

The Mohawk Council of Akwesasne describes a community along the St. Lawrence River divided by the Canada–United States boundary and the Ontario–Quebec boundary. Its account emphasizes continuing kinship across those divisions. The council’s own elected-government description is one institutional perspective within this community.

Read the sources [3] Mohawk Council of Akwesasne

04

A community museum’s interpretive role

Akwesasne Museum says its exhibits present Mohawk culture from Akwesasne people’s perspective. Its public account describes arts programmes and youth co-curation of a traveling exhibition. These examples show community participation in interpretation; they do not authorize copying collection objects or imply uniform practices across Mohawk communities.

Read the sources [4] Akwesasne Cultural Center / Akwesasne Museum

05

Language study at Six Nations

A Six Nations Polytechnic study conducted in 2016–2017 examined adult language-learning experience and coordination among programmes. Selected methods and project goals offer a second community context for Mohawk language work. Its recommendations remain attributed to that study, without a current speaker census or promised learning outcome.

Read the sources [5] Six Nations Polytechnic

About Us — selected Akwesasne community and council account ↗

The council introduces its elected community-government role and Akwesasne’s St. Lawrence River setting across international and provincial boundaries. It is a specifically situated Mohawk government account.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual introductory council-role and community/district paragraphs; selected About Akwesasne section identifying the St. Lawrence River, boundary divisions, kinship and other named Mohawk communities.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Museum — public community interpretation and arts programmes ↗

The museum explains how Akwesasne Mohawk people present their own cultural materials, sustain public arts programmes and involve youth in interpretation. It is an institution’s account of community cultural work.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual museum body: opening interpretive/collection paragraphs; traditional-arts programme description; basketry discussion; We Are From Akwesasne youth co-curation paragraph and closing community-planning statement.

Indigenous-ledSix Nations PolytechnicSource 5

Pathways to Creating Onkwehonwehnéha Speakers at Six Nations of The Grand River Territory — selected study sections ↗

A community-based 2016–2017 study examines adult language learning, programme coordination and opportunities to use language beyond classes. Its Six Nations focus is a specific community context, not a universal account of every Cayuga or Mohawk community.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual 96-page PDF: title/acknowledgments and abstract, PDF pp1–2 and7; selected background, project goals and study conduct pp8–11; selected focus-group/questionnaire methodology pp28–31.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026
